prelimsCapsule.coreConceptSummary: A Certificate of Deposit (CD) is a negotiable money market instrument issued in dematerialized form by banks and select All-India Financial Institutions (AIFIs) for funds deposited at the institution for a specified period. It acts as an unsecured, short-term promissory note, providing liquidity to investors and short-term capital for issuers.
highYieldFacts: Fact 1: CDs have a minimum maturity of 7 days and a maximum of 1 year for banks, while AIFIs can issue them for 1 year to 3 years.
Fact 2: They are issued in minimum denominations of Rs 5 lakh and in multiples of Rs 5 lakh thereafter.
Fact 3: CDs are transferable by endorsement and delivery, making them highly liquid instruments compared to term deposits.
Fact 4: Since 2021, RBI has permitted the issuance of CDs to individuals, corporations, companies, trusts, funds, and associations.
Fact 5: Banks are exempt from maintaining CRR and SLR on funds mobilized through CDs.
trapsAndElimination: Trap 1: Examiners often confuse CDs with Commercial Paper (CPs). Remember: CDs are issued by Banks/AIFIs, whereas CPs are issued by Corporates/NBFCs.
Trap 2: The maturity period differs significantly: Bank CDs max out at 1 year, whereas AIFI CDs can extend to 3 years.
keyArticlesOrStatutes: Reserve Bank of India (Certificate of Deposit) Directions, 2021

mainsFramework.inDepthTheoryHtml:
Evolution and Mechanics of Certificate of Deposit (CD)

The Certificate of Deposit (CD) is a pivotal instrument in India's money market, introduced in 1989 as part of the RBI's strategy to widen the range of money market instruments and give investors greater flexibility for the deployment of their short-term surplus liquidity.

Institutional Architecture

CDs are strictly regulated under the RBI (Certificate of Deposit) Directions, 2021. Unlike traditional fixed deposits, CDs are negotiable. This negotiability is the hallmark of its utility, allowing the holder to sell the instrument in the secondary market before maturity, thus serving as an alternative to call money or treasury bills for short-term parking of funds.

Contemporary Challenges & Governance

  • Interest Rate Sensitivity: During periods of tight liquidity, banks issue CDs at higher rates, increasing their Cost of Funds (CoF). This eventually impacts the Marginal Cost of Funds based Lending Rate (MCLR).
  • Financial Inclusion vs. Corporate Dominance: While retail participation is allowed, the high minimum denomination (Rs 5 lakh) essentially limits the instrument to HNI (High Net-worth Individuals) and institutional investors, keeping it out of reach for the retail common man.
  • Secondary Market Depth: Despite RBI initiatives, the secondary market for CDs remains relatively thin, with most investors holding them until maturity, which limits price discovery and liquidity depth.

dimensions.constitutional_or_legal: Regulated under the powers conferred by Section 45W of the RBI Act, 1934.
dimensions.socio_economic: High entry barriers restrict wealth management benefits to affluent sections, though it aids banking stability.
dimensions.administrative_governance: Supervised by RBI for liquidity management; ensures banks have alternative short-term funding routes.
dimensions.international_or_comparative: Aligns with global Basel III liquidity coverage requirements by fostering a robust money market.

landmarkJudgmentsOrReports: RBI Working Group on Money Market (Vaghul Committee recommendations on broadening instruments).

modelMainsQA.modelAnswerHtml:
Significance of Certificates of Deposit (CDs)

Certificates of Deposit serve as a crucial bridge in the Indian financial system by facilitating the transfer of liquidity from surplus units to deficit-ridden banks. They function as unsecured, negotiable money market instruments.

Role in Liquidity Management

  • Instrument for Banks: CDs allow banks to mobilize short-term funds without the rigidity of CASA (Current Account Savings Account) or traditional term deposits, especially during festive seasons or credit crunches.
  • Negotiability: Unlike standard term deposits, the secondary market transferability allows the holder to liquidate the investment, providing the holder with high flexibility.
  • CRR/SLR Exemption: Since they are treated as non-deposit liabilities, they help banks optimize their cost of funds by lowering the burden of mandatory reserve requirements.

Challenges in the Ecosystem

Despite their utility, the secondary market for CDs is primarily dominated by primary dealers and institutional buyers. The lack of retail participation, hindered by the Rs 5 lakh floor, limits the broad-basing of financial savings. Furthermore, volatility in the short-term interest rate cycle often leads to 'crowding out' where high bank CD rates pull liquidity away from corporate Commercial Papers (CPs).

Way Forward

To enhance the efficiency of the money market, the RBI should encourage the digitisation of CD trading platforms to improve transparency. Promoting a robust secondary market through incentivized market-making will provide better price discovery, aligning the Indian money market with international benchmarks of liquidity and stability, ultimately supporting the vision of a USD 5 trillion economy.

practiceMCQs.question: With reference to Certificate of Deposit (CD) in India, consider the following statements: 1. They are issued by banks at a discount to face value. 2. They are negotiable instruments which can be traded in the secondary market.
practiceMCQs.explanation: CDs are indeed issued at a discount (or floating rate) and are inherently negotiable instruments.

practiceMCQs.question: Which of the following entities are permitted to issue Certificate of Deposit (CD) as per current RBI regulations?
practiceMCQs.explanation: Only Scheduled Commercial Banks and select AIFIs are permitted to issue CDs. NBFCs are not permitted to issue CDs.
